title: Quiz & Games
description: Speed rounds, timed challenges, myth-busting, matching games and a media timeline – revise fast and beat your high score.
intro: Quick, competitive revision. Timed quizzes give points for correct answers and a bonus for speed, and your best score is saved on this device. Challenge a classmate to beat it!

exercises.title: Speed round: key facts
exercises.instruction: Answer as many questions as you can before the timer runs out. You get points for every correct answer and a bonus for the time left.

questions.prompt: Which EU regulation has protected personal data since 2018?
questions.explanation: The General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) has applied since May 2018.

questions.prompt: Who popularised the term “filter bubble”?
questions.explanation: Eli Pariser, in his 2011 book The Filter Bubble.

questions.prompt: What does Reporters Without Borders (RSF) publish every year?
options: A list of fake news websites
A ranking of social media platforms
questions.explanation: RSF has published the World Press Freedom Index annually since 2002.

questions.prompt: False information spread deliberately to deceive is called …
questions.explanation: Disinformation = false + intent to deceive or harm.

questions.prompt: Collins Dictionary’s Word of the Year 2017 was …
questions.explanation: “Fake news”. (“Post-truth” was Oxford’s Word of the Year 2016.)

questions.prompt: Whose legal cases led the EU’s top court to strike down Safe Harbour and the Privacy Shield?
questions.explanation: The Austrian privacy activist Max Schrems.

questions.prompt: What is the first step of the SIFT method?
questions.explanation: SIFT = Stop, Investigate the source, Find better coverage, Trace claims to their original context.

questions.prompt: A one-sided feeling of closeness to an influencer is called a …
questions.explanation: Parasocial relationship.

questions.prompt: In the 2018 MIT study, who was mainly responsible for spreading false news faster?
questions.explanation: Bots spread true and false news at similar rates; humans made the difference.

questions.prompt: Which EU law bans “dark patterns” on online platforms?
questions.explanation: The Digital Services Act (DSA).

exercises.title: Vocabulary blitz
exercises.instruction: Sixty seconds, ten questions. How many can you get right?

questions.prompt: A video that spreads very fast online goes …
questions.explanation: go viral

questions.prompt: The opposite of “biased” is …
questions.explanation: impartial = not supporting any side

questions.prompt: To “debunk” a claim means to …
questions.explanation: debunk = show that something is false

questions.prompt: A person who reveals wrongdoing inside an organisation is a …
questions.explanation: whistle-blower

questions.prompt: “The platform took the post down.” means it …
questions.explanation: take down = remove

questions.prompt: Which is correct?
questions.explanation: “Information” is uncountable.

questions.prompt: “Doomscrolling” means …
questions.explanation: doom + scrolling

questions.prompt: Journalists hold the powerful to …
questions.explanation: hold someone to account

questions.prompt: The noun of “anonymous” is …
questions.explanation: anonymity

questions.prompt: Clickbait is mainly designed to …
questions.explanation: Clickbait prioritises clicks over information.

exercises.title: The 2-minute challenge
exercises.instruction: Extra challenge: fifteen harder questions mixing facts, vocabulary, grammar and critical thinking. You have two minutes.

questions.prompt: “Everyone uses this app, so it must be fine.” Which fallacy is this?
questions.explanation: Appeal to popularity (bandwagon).

questions.prompt: No sooner ___ the post gone live than it was shared thousands of times.
questions.explanation: No sooner + had + subject + past participle.

questions.prompt: The “liar’s dividend” means that …
options: liars earn money from fake news
genuine evidence can be dismissed as fake
questions.explanation: Because fakes exist, real evidence can be denied.

questions.prompt: Which of these is NOT a right under the GDPR?
questions.explanation: The GDPR is about personal data, not about internet access.

questions.prompt: Platforms should be responsible ___ what they recommend.
questions.explanation: responsible for

questions.prompt: “Astroturfing” is …
questions.explanation: Astroturf is artificial grass – a campaign made to look like genuine public support.

questions.prompt: Jonathan Haidt’s 2024 book is called …
questions.explanation: The Anxious Generation.

questions.prompt: Which court struck down the EU–US Privacy Shield in 2020?
options: The Court of Justice of the European Union
The European Court of Human Rights
questions.explanation: The Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU), in the “Schrems II” case.

questions.prompt: “False balance” in reporting means …
options: presenting unequal positions as equally valid
questions.explanation: E.g. giving a fringe view the same weight as a strong scientific consensus.

questions.prompt: If I ___ the source, I wouldn’t have shared the post.
questions.explanation: Third conditional: if + past perfect.

questions.prompt: The aim of a SLAPP is to …
questions.explanation: Strategic lawsuit against public participation.

questions.prompt: “Prebunking” means …
options: warning people about manipulation techniques in advance
questions.explanation: Pre-emptive debunking, also called inoculation.

questions.prompt: German “eventuell” means …
questions.explanation: A classic false friend: eventually = schließlich.

questions.prompt: Which feature did its designer, Aza Raskin, later say he regretted?
questions.explanation: Infinite scroll.

questions.prompt: Content credentials (e.g. C2PA) attach information about …
options: a file’s origin and editing history
questions.explanation: They record how and by whom a file was created or edited.

exercises.title: Fact or myth?
exercises.instruction: Is each statement a fact or a myth? Some of these myths are repeated so often that many people believe them.

questions.prompt: “Only 7 per cent of communication is verbal.”
questions.explanation: A misinterpretation of Albert Mehrabian’s experiments, which only concerned judging feelings when signals contradict each other.

questions.prompt: “GDPR fines can be higher than 20 million euros.”
questions.explanation: Fines can reach 4 % of worldwide annual turnover if that is higher than 20 million euros.

questions.prompt: “In the MIT study, bots were the main reason why false news spread faster.”
questions.explanation: Bots spread true and false news at similar rates; humans were mainly responsible.

questions.prompt: “The internet and the World Wide Web are the same thing.”
questions.explanation: The internet is the global network; the Web (invented by Tim Berners-Lee in 1989) is one service that runs on it, like email.

questions.prompt: “Once you delete a post, it is gone forever.”
questions.explanation: Screenshots, copies and archives can keep content alive.

questions.prompt: “Private or incognito browsing makes you anonymous to the websites you visit.”
questions.explanation: Incognito mode mainly stops your browser from saving history on your device. Websites, employers or internet providers can still see your activity.

questions.prompt: “In the EU, influencers must clearly label paid content as advertising.”
questions.explanation: Commercial communication must be recognisable as such.

questions.prompt: “Professional fact-checkers often leave a website quickly to see what other sources say about it.”
questions.explanation: This is called lateral reading.

exercises.title: Who’s who in media debates?
exercises.instruction: Match each person with the idea, work or event they are known for. Mentioning a name and idea correctly in the exam shows real background knowledge.

pairs.right: privacy cases against Facebook at the EU’s top court
Reclaiming Conversation – texting vs. face-to-face talk
“a wealth of information creates a poverty of attention”
The Anxious Generation – phones and teen mental health

exercises.explanation: Use names carefully in the exam: “As the scholar Shoshana Zuboff has argued, …” sounds impressive – but only if you are sure of the facts.

exercises.title: Acronym match
exercises.instruction: Match the acronyms with their full forms.
exercises.explanation: RSF comes from the French name: Reporters sans frontières. In the exam, say the full form the first time you use an acronym.

exercises.title: Media timeline
exercises.instruction: Put these milestones in media history in chronological order, starting with the earliest.
items: Gutenberg’s printing press spreads in Europe (15th century)
Television becomes a mass medium in many Western countries (1950s)
Tim Berners-Lee proposes the World Wide Web (1989)
ChatGPT is released to the public (2022)
exercises.explanation: Each new medium has triggered both hopes and fears. Comparing today’s debates about smartphones or AI with earlier debates about radio or TV can be a sophisticated point in your exam.

exercises.title: Fact or opinion?
exercises.instruction: Sort each statement: is it a verifiable fact (it can be checked) or an opinion / value judgement?

items.text: The GDPR has applied in the EU since 2018.
Collins Dictionary chose “fake news” as its Word of the Year in 2017.
Australia has passed a law setting a minimum age of 16 for accounts on many social media platforms.
Tim Berners-Lee invented the World Wide Web.
Social media is the worst invention of the century.
Influencers should be ashamed of themselves.
Printed newspapers are more pleasant to read than news apps.
Every school ought to ban phones.
items.explanation: “Ought to / should” usually signals a value judgement.

exercises.explanation: A fact can be checked and proved true or false. An opinion expresses a judgement or preference. Watch out: a fact can be false (it is still a factual claim), and opinions can be well or badly argued.

exercises.title: Odd one out
exercises.instruction: Which word does NOT belong with the others? Think about meaning, not spelling.

questions.prompt: debunk – verify – fact-check – fabricate
questions.explanation: The other three are about establishing the truth; fabricate = invent something false.

questions.prompt: viral – trending – obsolete – popular
questions.explanation: Obsolete = out of date, no longer used.

questions.prompt: impartial – objective – biased – neutral
questions.explanation: Biased is the opposite of the other three.

questions.prompt: privacy – anonymity – confidentiality – publicity
questions.explanation: Publicity = public attention; the others are about keeping information private.

questions.prompt: mislead – deceive – manipulate – inform
questions.explanation: Inform is neutral or positive; the others describe dishonest influence.

questions.prompt: censor – suppress – silence – amplify
questions.explanation: Amplify = make louder or spread more widely.

exercises.title: How apps keep you hooked
exercises.instruction: Match each design feature with its effect on users.

pairs.right: starts the next video before you decide to watch it
pull you back into the app
turn social approval into a visible number
make taking a break feel like losing something

exercises.explanation: Being able to name and explain specific design features makes your argument about the attention economy much more convincing than saying “apps are addictive”.

exercises.title: Name the concept
exercises.instruction: Read each scenario and choose the concept it illustrates.

questions.prompt: A political party pays hundreds of people to post “spontaneous” messages of support online.
questions.explanation: Fake grassroots support = astroturfing.

questions.prompt: A TV show presents a climate scientist and a climate-change denier as equally credible experts.
questions.explanation: Giving equal weight to unequal positions = false balance.

questions.prompt: You stop watching the news because it makes you feel anxious and powerless.
questions.explanation: Deliberately avoiding news = news avoidance.

questions.prompt: Before an election, short videos teach people to recognise common manipulation tricks.
questions.explanation: Warning people in advance = prebunking.

questions.prompt: On a website, the “Accept all” button is big and colourful, while “Reject” is hidden in small grey text.
questions.explanation: A design that pressures you into a choice = dark pattern.

questions.prompt: A real photo from a 2015 flood is shared as if it showed a flood that happened yesterday.
options: A cheapfake / content out of context
questions.explanation: A genuine image in a false context, without AI manipulation.
